chunks.heading: COLLISION DETECTION: DISCRETE VS. CONTINUOUS
chunks.content:
COLLISION DETECTION: DISCRETE VS. CONTINUOUS
If you look at the Rigidbody component, you'll see that there is a pop-up menu for
selecting Collision Detection. By setting the collisionDetectionMode of a Rigid-
body, we're setting the same thing. Here's an explanation for the different values:
■ Discrete: The Rigidbody only checks collisions in each FixedUpdate. This
is the most efficient, but it also can mean that if a fast-moving projectile is
on one side of a thin wall in one FixedUpdate and on the other side in the
next FixedUpdate (but doesn't touch the wall in either frame), discrete
mode will not see the collision at all.
■ Continuous: This is more accurate for fast-moving objects like the pro-
jectile because it checks for collisions in between FixedUpdates. However,
it takes more processor power to do this.
■ Continuous Dynamic: If you were making a billiards game with several
fast-moving balls, each ball would need to be set to Continuous Dynamic
in order to collide accurately with the others. This is because the preced-
ing Continuous mode only checks the moving object against the static
(unmoving) positions of other objects in the frame. Continuous Dynamic
is needed when you want to see if two fast-moving objects collide with
each other. This, of course, takes significantly more processing power
than any other mode.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
CodInG the PrototyPe 699
■ Continuous Speculative: This mode is needed if you want to treat
a kinematic Rigidbody as if it has Continuous collision detection. The
other forms of Continuous collision detection rely on the velocity of the
Rigidbody to check for collisions between frames, but a kinematic Rigid-
body doesn't use its velocity, so Continuous Speculative uses different
calculations to speculate (i.e., guess) at what the kinematic Rigidbody hit
between frames. This is actually less processor-intensive than the other
forms of Continuous detection, but it is also less accurate.
In prior editions of the book, we just set the Collision Detection for the Projectile
to Continuous and left it at that, but in more recent versions of Unity, if you set a
Rigidbody with Continuous collision detection to is.inePatic, Unity will throw a
warning into the Console, so I wanted to show you how to set collisionDetection-
Mode in code and avoid this warning.
For more information about the types of collision detection, click the help icon in
the top-right corner of the Rigidbody component.

As you can see in Figure 30.8, vectors are added and subtracted one component at a
time (meaning that the x and y dimensions are handled separately). The figure is two
dimensional, but the same methods work for 3D. The x components of the vectors A
and B are subtracted independently from the y components, making a new Vector2
that is Vector2( 2-5, 8-3 ), which becomes Vector2( -3, 5 ). The figure illustrates that A-B
gives us the vector distance between A and B (with the vector's root at [0,0], also known

move to get from point B to point A. A mnemonic to remember which one the vector
will point at is "A minus B looks at A."

Making a Follow Camera
You need _MainCamera to follow the projectile when it is launched, but the behavior is
a little more complicated than that. The eventual full behavior should be as follows:
A. The camera sits at an initial position and doesn't move during Slingshot's
aimingMode.
B. After the projectile is launched, the camera follows it (with a little easing to make it
follow the projectile with a bit of a smooth lag; we'll cover this soon).
C. As the camera moves up into the air, increase the Camera.orthographicSize to keep
the ground in view.
D. When the projectile comes to rest, the camera stops following it and returns to the
initial position.
To begin with, let's just get the camera moving at all, and we'll iteratively add more
functionality as we go. The following code will enable the camera to follow a POI (Point
of Interest) GameObject. We will later set that POI in the Slingshot code.
1. Select _MainCamera in the Hierarchy.
2. To create a new FollowCam script and add it to _MainCamera at the same time:
a. Click the Add Component button at the bottom of the _MainCamera Inspector.
b. Type FollowCam into the search bar that appears. This will not find a pre-
existing FollowCam script, so it will give you the option to create a new script.
c. Click New script.
d. Double-check the FollowCam name and then click Create and Add.
The process in step 2 will create a new FollowCam script in the Assets folder of the Proj-
ect pane and also add that FollowCam script to _MainCamera as a Component. This is a
newer workflow in Unity that I've personally been using a lot. The only negative is that
it places the new script in the top-level of the Assets folder in the Project pane, so you

Issue B: The Projectile Doesn't Bounce Realistically
To fix issue B, you must add both Rigidbody constraints and a Physic Material to the
Projectile prefab:
1. Select the Projectile prefab in the Project pane.
2. In the Projectile Rigidbody component:
a. Open the disclosure triangle next to Constraints.
b. Set the check box next to Freeze Position Z to true.
c. Set the check boxes next to Freeze Rotation X, Y, and Z to true.
Freeze Position Z keeps the projectile from moving toward or away from the camera
(basically keeping it in the same Z depth as both the ground and the castle that will be
added later). Freeze Rotation X, Y, and Z keeps it from rolling around.
3. Save the scene, click Play, and try launching the projectile again.
These Rigidbody settings keep the projectile from rolling endlessly, but it still doesn't
feel right. You've spent your whole life experiencing physics, and that gives you an intui-
tive feel for the kinds of behaviors that feel like natural, real-world physics. This is true
for your players as well, which means that even though physics is a complex system that
requires a lot of math to model, if you make your game physics feel like the physics that
players are used to, you won't have to explain that math to them. Adding a Physic Mate-
rial can make your physically simulated objects feel a lot more realistic.
4. From the Unity menu bar, choose Assets > Create > Physic Material.
5. Name this Physic material PhysMat_Projectile.

ENUM
An enum (or enumeration) is a way of defining specific, named numbers in C#.
The enum definition at the top of the MissionDemolition C# script declares an
enum type GaPeMode with three potential values: idle, playing, and leYelEnd.
After you define an enum, you can then declare a variable that uses the defined
enum as its type.
public GameMode mode = GameMode.idle;
The preceding line creates a new variable named Pode that is of the type
GaPeMode and has the value GaPeMode.idle.
You often use enums in code when only a few specific options exist for a variable
and you want those options to be easily readable by humans. Alternatively, passing
the type of game mode as a string (e.g., "idle", "playing", or "levelEnd") would be
possible, but the enum is a much cleaner way of doing this that isn't as susceptible
to misspelling and that allows for autocomplete while typing.
For more information about enums, see Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."

I am always on the lookout for any time that it feels like the controller, keyboard, mouse,

That's it for the Mission Demolition prototype. In just one chapter, you've made a

Next Steps
You could add a ton of additional features, some of which include the following:
■ Use PlayerPrefs to store the best score, as you did in Apple Picker. In this game, it
would probably be scored like Golf where the player is trying to complete all levels
in as few shots as possible.
■ Make the castle parts out of various materials, some of which would have more or
less mass. Some materials could even break if struck hard enough (by break, I mean
disappear; actual destructible meshes are very complex to implement). When work-
ing with materials like this, don't forget that you can use a Physic Material to choose
how bouncy a Collider is.
■ Use a Line Renderer to draw the rubber band of the slingshot.
■ Add more background elements like mountains or buildings, and implement
movement or even actual parallax scrolling on the background clouds. You could
also tie that parallax scrolling to the scale and z position of the clouds, with larger
clouds closer and faster moving while smaller clouds would be further away and
move more slowly. We will implement simple parallax scrolling Chapter 32, "Space
SHMUP – Part 2."
■ Anything else you want!
After you've worked your way through the other prototypes in this book, come back
to this one and think about what you could add to it. Create your own designs, show
them to people, and iterate to make the game better. Remember that design is always
an iterative process. If you make a change you don't like, don't let it discourage you; just
chalk it up to experience and try something else.
It's also worth repeating here that it's okay if you don't completely understand every-
thing that we did in the code in this chapter. I often liken learning C# to learning any
normal human language, while also solving a bunch of logic puzzles. When learning
Spanish, Mandarin, or French, there is a lot of repetition, some of which you're not
going to understand at the time, but immersion within that language and seeing it used
will help you to eventually learn it much better (and faster!). These tutorials are that kind
of repetition for Unity and C#. It's okay if you don't understand exactly what's going on
with each step as long as you get the general idea. Later, when you want to do some-
thing like add a trail behind a moving GameObject that is more configurable than a
standard Trail Renderer would allow, you'll remember this project and can return to it to
copy and modify how we did it here.

The SHMUP (or shoot 'em up) game genre
includes such classic games as Galaga and
Galaxian from the 1980s and the more modern

In this chapter, you create a SHMUP using
several programming techniques that will
serve you well throughout your programming
and prototyping careers. These include class
inheritance, static fields and methods, the
singleton pattern, and delegates. Though
you've seen many of these techniques before,
you will use them more extensively in this
prototype.
